newsitem.title: RWANDA: Refugees trickle back as Rwanda rejects force.
newsitem.headline: Refugees trickle back as Rwanda rejects force.

text.p: The Rwandan government said on Monday it did not want any multinational military force intended to help feed refugees in eastern Zaire to be based in Rwanda, insisting its mission was irrelevant.
"Rwanda's position is any foreign force is irrelevant because the bulk of the refugees have returned," said Claude Dusaidi, an adviser to Rwandan military strongman Paul Kagame.
"Instead of sending a force, they should send humanitarian aid to Rwanda to help the returnees settle here," he said.
Refugees continued to trickle over the border from Goma in Zaire, north of Lake Kivu, and the U.N. refugee agency UNHCR said "thousands" more were reported to be on the way.
UNHCR spokesman Ray Wilkinson said around 600 refugees had arrived in Sake, 20 kms (12 miles) west of Goma, from the camps around Bukavu at the southern tip of the lake.
"Our local staff have been told by them that thousands, possibly tens of thousands, of others are behind them," he said.
Western and African military officials who met in Stuttgart over the weekend agreed on scenarios to help feed the refugees in Zaire but there seemed no real urgency to the mission.
Support for the Canadian-led mission, authorised by the United Nations, has waned because some 600,000 Hutu refugees have returned home to Rwanda since mid-November.

Canadian Prime Minister Jean Chretien said on Monday that military intervention may still be needed, but that a force as small as 1,000 people could be enough, rather than the 10-15,000 mooted earlier.
Chretien told a news conference in the Philippines: "My judgement is we don't need 10,000 people. It might be more in the range of 1,000 or 1,500."
But French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette criticised the international community for dragging its feet.
"Is it because they are African that the international community is less interested," he told reporters at a meeting of European Union foreign ministers in Brussels.
"I am frankly shocked when I see that kind of apathy hiding behind endless discussions," he said. "It is urgent. The French position is that the international force...is more than ever necessary."
The UNHCR's Wilkinson said refugees heading for the border reported fighting south of Sake, and on the road to the Masisi.
Refugees arriving at Mugunga camp outside Goma bore wounds from fighting in the Masisi region, northwest of Lake Kivu.
"We are getting a lot of very serious wounds," said Nicholas Krzamiem of the International Federation of the Red Cross at a way-station set up at the entrance to Mugunga camp.

"A lot of them are machete wounds, bullets, sticks and stones. These are people being attacked as they are trying to break away from groups of refugees being herded through the forests by former Rwandan Hutu militiamen."
The refugees who have returned to Rwanda have gone to flee fighting between Zairean rebels, the Zairean army and the Rwandan Hutu hardliners.
They had left in 1994 after a Tutsi-led army overran the country following the genocide of Tutsis by the Hutu militia.
